Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers with a fixed, finite number of significant bits, so most sums must be rounded to fit back into that representation. When you add two floating-point numbers, the exact mathematical result is fitted to the nearest representable value, and that rounding step discards information. If you then add a third number, the outcome depends on which two numbers were combined first, because the intermediate rounding error introduced at each step propagates differently depending on the order of operations. Mathematically, (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c) for real numbers, but in floating-point arithmetic these two expressions can produce different bit patterns because the rounding that occurs after computing a + b is not the same as the rounding that occurs after computing b + c. This is especially pronounced when the operands have very different magnitudes, since adding a small number to a much larger one can cause the small number's contribution to be partially or entirely lost to rounding, whereas summing several small numbers together first, before adding the large one, can preserve more of their combined magnitude.

This lack of associativity becomes practically important in large matrix multiplications because each output element is the sum of many products, and the specific order in which those products are added is not fixed by the mathematical definition of matrix multiplication—it depends on implementation choices. Modern hardware amplifies this variability: GPUs and multi-core CPUs parallelize reductions by splitting the sum into chunks that are computed by different threads or vector lanes and then combined, and the order of that combination can vary depending on thread scheduling, tile sizes, block partitioning, and even the specific kernel or library version used. Techniques like Kahan summation, tree-based reductions, or pairwise summation each accumulate rounding error differently. As a result, running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, different numbers of threads, or even different runs on the same hardware if the scheduler assigns work nondeterministically, can yield results that differ in the last few bits of precision. For most numerical purposes these differences are negligible, but they matter for reproducibility: two runs of the same program that are expected to produce bit-identical results may not, complicating debugging, scientific replication, and validation of machine learning training pipelines, where accumulated small discrepancies can eventually diverge into materially different model weights or outputs, especially over many iterations or when combined with nonlinear operations that amplify small numerical differences.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a finite number of significand bits, so the exact mathematical sum of two representable values is often not itself representable. The hardware therefore rounds each intermediate result to the nearest representable value, and this rounding is where associativity breaks down. Consider adding a very large number, a very small number, and the negation of the large number. If the large numbers are added first, they cancel exactly and the small number survives intact. If instead the large number is added to the small one first, the small quantity may fall entirely below the least significant bit of the large value's significand and be discarded by rounding; the subsequent cancellation then yields zero. The two groupings, mathematically identical, give different answers. More generally, every addition contributes a rounding error whose magnitude is proportional to the size of the intermediate partial sum, so an ordering that produces large intermediate values accumulates larger absolute error than one that keeps partial sums small. Summing a long series of similarly sized positive numbers sequentially, for example, grows the running total until later addends are relatively tiny and are partially or wholly lost, whereas pairwise or tree-shaped summation keeps the magnitudes of operands comparable and loses far less. Additional wrinkles arise from gradual underflow, from operations that are internally computed at higher precision such as fused multiply-add, and from denormal handling, all of which can make one ordering more accurate or less accurate than another in ways that depend on the data.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, and each dot product is a reduction over the shared dimension. Any high-performance implementation is free to reorganise that reduction. Blocking for cache locality splits the shared dimension into tiles whose partial results are accumulated in some particular order. Vectorised kernels keep several independent accumulators in vector lanes and combine them only at the end, which is a tree reduction rather than a sequential one. Multithreaded and multi-GPU implementations split the reduction across workers and merge partial sums in an order that may depend on scheduling, on how many threads happen to be available, or on the arrival order of atomic updates. Autotuned libraries select different kernels for different problem shapes and different hardware generations. Each of these choices is a different grouping of the same sum, and therefore a different rounding trajectory.

The practical consequence is that the same mathematical product computed twice can differ in its low-order bits. The discrepancy is usually tiny, on the order of the unit roundoff times the magnitude of the intermediate sums, but it is not zero, and it is amplified when cancellation occurs or when results are fed through iterative or chaotic processes such as training loops or long simulations. Bitwise reproducibility across machines, thread counts, or library versions therefore cannot be assumed unless the implementation explicitly fixes the reduction order, which typically costs performance. Where exact repeatability matters, one must pin the algorithm and the parallel decomposition, use deterministic reduction modes, or employ compensated or exact accumulation techniques.

Floating-point numbers are represented with a fixed number of significant bits, so most real numbers must be rounded to the nearest representable value after every arithmetic operation. Addition on modern hardware follows the IEEE 754 standard, which guarantees that each individual operation is correctly rounded, but it says nothing about the result of combining many operations in different orders. Because each addition can introduce a small rounding error, and because the magnitude of that error depends on the relative sizes of the two operands being combined, the order in which numbers are summed changes which intermediate values get rounded and by how much. Adding a small number to a much larger one, for instance, can cause the small number's low-order bits to be lost entirely, whereas summing several small numbers together first and only then adding the large one preserves more of that information. As a result, (a + b) + c does not generally equal a + (b + c) in floating-point arithmetic, even though it would in exact real-number arithmetic. This lack of associativity is a direct consequence of finite precision and rounding, not a flaw in any particular processor, but it is exposed differently by different hardware because processors and libraries choose different orders of evaluation to maximize throughput.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large number of dot products, each of which is a sum of many products, so it is exactly the kind of computation where associativity matters. On a CPU, a GPU, or a specialized accelerator, the way that sum is decomposed into partial sums depends on the hardware's parallelism, vector width, memory layout, and scheduling. GPUs, for example, often split a long reduction across many threads or warps, combine results using tree-like reductions, and may use fused multiply-add instructions that change rounding behavior compared to separate multiply and add steps. Different GPU models, different thread-block sizes, different numbers of parallel units, or even different runs where the operating system schedules threads differently can all lead to sums being accumulated in different orders. Because floating-point addition is not associative, these different orders produce numerically different results, even though all of them are "correct" in the sense of satisfying the rounding rules of IEEE 754 at each step. The discrepancies are usually tiny, on the order of the machine epsilon per operation, but they can accumulate over many additions, especially in deep neural network training where the same matrix multiplications are repeated across many layers and iterations. This means that running identical code on different hardware, or even the same hardware with different parallel configurations, can yield slightly different final results, making bit-for-bit reproducibility of large-scale floating-point computations difficult to guarantee without explicitly fixing the reduction order.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a fixed number of significand bits, so most arithmetic results cannot be represented exactly and must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition on such a format is commutative — the rounding of a+b does not depend on the order of the operands — but it is not associative, because rounding happens after every individual operation, and the amount of information discarded depends on the relative magnitudes of the values being combined at that moment. If you add a very large number to a very small one, the small one's low-order bits fall off the end of the significand and are lost forever; whether that loss occurs depends on what has already been accumulated. The classic illustration is adding a huge value, its negation, and a tiny value: grouping the huge pair first cancels them exactly and preserves the tiny value, while adding the huge value to the tiny one first annihilates the tiny contribution entirely, leaving a different final answer. Similar effects arise more subtly whenever partial sums grow large relative to the terms still to be added, so long accumulations tend to lose accuracy progressively, and reordering them changes which digits survive.

Matrix multiplication is built almost entirely from such accumulations: each output element is a sum of many products, and a large multiplication involves an enormous number of these sums. High-performance implementations do not evaluate them in the naive left-to-right order. They tile the computation to fit caches and registers, split the inner dimension into chunks processed by separate vector lanes, threads, or GPU blocks, and then combine partial results in whatever order the hardware and scheduler make convenient. They may also use fused multiply-add instructions, which round once instead of twice, or wider internal accumulators, or Strassen-like algebraic rearrangements. Every one of these choices fixes a particular reduction order, and different orders produce results that differ in the last few bits.

The practical consequence is that the "same" matrix multiplication can yield bitwise different answers when run on a different number of threads, on a different GPU, with a different library version, or even twice on the same machine if atomic accumulation or dynamic work-stealing makes the order nondeterministic from run to run. These tiny discrepancies are usually harmless in magnitude, but they are not harmless in effect: iterative solvers may take different numbers of steps, branches conditioned on comparisons may diverge, and in deep networks the differences amplify across layers and training steps, so two runs can end up in visibly different states. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, or using compensated or exactly-rounded summation, both of which cost performance.

Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers using a finite number of bits, typically following the IEEE 754 standard, which allocates a fixed number of bits to the mantissa (significand) and exponent. When two floating-point numbers of very different magnitudes are added, the smaller number must be shifted to align its exponent with the larger one, and in this process some of its low-order bits may fall off the end of the mantissa and be rounded away. The result is that each addition operation introduces a small rounding error, and critically, the size and direction of that error depends on the relative magnitudes of the two operands being combined. Because of this, (a + b) + c need not equal a + (b + c): the intermediate rounded sums differ depending on which numbers are added first, so the order of operations changes which bits get truncated and thus changes the final result, sometimes only in the last bit, but sometimes more substantially if catastrophic cancellation or large magnitude disparities are involved.

This property becomes highly consequential in large matrix multiplications, which fundamentally require computing many long sums of products—dot products between rows and columns whose length equals the shared dimension of the matrices. When this dimension is large, say in the thousands or millions as in deep learning workloads, the accumulation of these products is a substantial reduction operation. On modern hardware, the order in which these products are summed is not fixed by the mathematical definition of matrix multiplication but rather by the specific implementation: different CPU architectures, GPU kernels, BLAS libraries, thread counts, tile sizes, and vectorization strategies all lead to different groupings and orderings of the underlying additions. A GPU might sum values in parallel across many cores using tree reductions, while a CPU might sum sequentially or in blocks matched to cache line sizes; even the same GPU model running the same code twice can produce different reduction orders when nondeterministic scheduling or atomic operations are involved.

As a result, numerically identical mathematical operations—the same matrices multiplied together—can yield bitwise different outputs depending on the hardware, the library version, the number of threads, or even runtime scheduling decisions. This lack of bit-for-bit reproducibility complicates scientific research and machine learning workflows that depend on exact determinism, such as debugging, verifying checkpoint restarts, or auditing results across different machines. While these discrepancies are usually minuscule in isolation, they can compound over many layers of a neural network or many iterations of an algorithm, occasionally leading to divergent trajectories in chaotic or ill-conditioned computations, which is why specialized deterministic algorithms or fixed reduction orders are sometimes enforced when exact reproducibility matters more than raw performance.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a fixed number of significand bits, so most real values, and most results of arithmetic on them, cannot be represented exactly. Every operation therefore produces the exactly-correct result rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition is still commutative, because rounding depends only on the exact sum, which does not care about operand order. Associativity, however, fails, because grouping changes which intermediate results get rounded and how much information is discarded along the way. The classic illustration uses a large value and two small ones: if you add a huge number to a tiny number, the tiny number may fall entirely below the last bit of the large one and vanish, so adding two tiny numbers to a huge one in sequence loses both, while summing the two tiny numbers first can produce a value big enough to survive the final addition. In double precision, adding one to a quantity near 2^53 and then subtracting that quantity yields zero, whereas subtracting first and then adding one yields one. Catastrophic cancellation compounds this: when nearly equal quantities are subtracted, the leading digits annihilate and whatever rounding error was already present is promoted into the leading digits of the answer, so tiny order-dependent discrepancies can be amplified without bound in badly conditioned sums.

Matrix multiplication is nothing but a very large collection of dot products, and a dot product is a sum of many products that must be reduced to a single number. The mathematical result is independent of the order of that reduction, but the computed result is not. High-performance implementations choose reduction orders for speed, not for a canonical ordering: they tile the loops to fit cache hierarchies, split the accumulation dimension into chunks handled by different threads or different GPU blocks whose partial sums are combined in whatever order they finish, use vector registers that maintain several independent partial accumulators interleaved across lanes, unroll loops to expose instruction-level parallelism, fuse multiply and add so that a product escapes an intermediate rounding, and sometimes substitute Strassen-like algorithms or lower-precision accumulation with block-wise correction. Each of these choices induces a different parenthesization, and therefore a different pattern of rounding, so the same two matrices multiplied on a different number of threads, a different core count, a different vector width, a different library version, or a different accelerator can yield results that differ in the last few bits.

Those last few bits matter in practice. Bitwise-identical outputs are what make regression tests, debugging, and scientific replication tractable, and small divergences can be amplified by iterative solvers, chaotic dynamics, or discrete decisions like comparisons and argmax, so two runs may take different branches and diverge visibly. Remedies include fixing thread counts and reduction trees, requiring deterministic library modes, using compensated or exactly-rounded summation, or accumulating in wider precision, all of which trade throughput for reproducibility.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a fixed number of significant bits, so most real values must be rounded to the nearest representable neighbour. Addition therefore consists of two steps: computing the exact mathematical sum of two approximations, and then rounding that sum back into the format. It is this second step that destroys associativity. When we compute (a + b) + c, the intermediate result a + b is rounded before c is added, and information that fell below the precision threshold is discarded permanently. When we compute a + (b + c), a different intermediate is rounded, and a different set of low-order bits is lost. The two results can differ by an amount on the order of the rounding error of the larger intermediate. The classic illustration uses a very large number, its negation, and a small number: in double precision, (1e16 + 1) - 1e16 evaluates to zero because adding one to 1e16 cannot change any stored bit, whereas 1e16 + (1 - 1e16) evaluates to exactly one. The magnitude of the discrepancy grows with the dynamic range of the summands and with cancellation, where two nearly equal quantities subtract and leave a small difference whose relative error has been amplified by the earlier rounding.

Matrix multiplication is built from dot products, and a dot product is a long chain of additions whose order the programmer usually does not specify. Modern hardware and libraries exploit this freedom aggressively. A vector unit with eight lanes maintains eight partial sums and combines them only at the end, which is a tree reduction rather than a sequential one. A multithreaded implementation splits the summation index across cores and adds their contributions in whatever order they finish, or in a fixed but implementation-defined order. Cache blocking chops the reduction dimension into tiles and accumulates tile by tile. GPUs perform warp-level shuffles and atomic accumulation whose ordering depends on scheduling. Fused multiply-add instructions add a further wrinkle by keeping the product at full width before rounding, so a kernel that uses FMA and one that does not will disagree even at identical addition order. Tensor cores and mixed-precision paths accumulate in a different format again.

The practical consequence is that the same mathematical product computed on two machines, with two thread counts, with two library versions, or even twice on the same GPU, can differ in the last few bits. Individually these differences are within the expected error bound and harmless, but they are not nothing: iterated through many layers of a neural network, through an eigenvalue solver, or through a branch that tests a sign, they can amplify into visibly divergent outputs. Bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, for instance by pinning thread counts and library versions, disabling nondeterministic kernels, or using compensated or fixed-point accumulation, usually at some cost in speed.

Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers with a finite number of bits of precision, typically following the IEEE 754 standard, which allocates a fixed number of bits for the mantissa. When two floating-point numbers of very different magnitudes are added, the smaller number's least significant bits may extend beyond what the mantissa can represent, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. This rounding step is where associativity breaks down: the expression (a + b) + c can produce a different rounding path, and therefore a different final result, than a + (b + c), because the intermediate sums differ depending on the order in which the additions occur, and each addition introduces its own independent rounding error. Mathematically, real-number addition is associative, but the rounded, finite-precision version implemented in hardware is not, since rounding is a nonlinear operation that depends on the specific values being combined at each step.

This has direct consequences for large matrix multiplications, which fundamentally involve computing many long sums, specifically the dot products between rows and columns that produce each output element. When multiplying large matrices, an entry in the result is the sum of potentially thousands or millions of products, and the order in which those products are added can vary depending on the algorithm, the hardware architecture, the degree of parallelism, and even the specific compiler optimizations or math library implementation used. Modern hardware often performs these reductions using multiple threads, vector instructions, or specialized accelerators like GPUs and tensor cores, all of which may split the summation into chunks that are combined in parallel and then merged, rather than accumulating strictly left to right. Because the reduction order is not fixed and can change based on how work is scheduled across cores or how a library chooses to tile the computation, the rounding errors accumulate differently each time, leading to results that differ in their least significant bits between runs, between hardware platforms, or even between different invocations on the same machine if nondeterministic scheduling is involved.

For applications where bitwise reproducibility matters, such as scientific computing, debugging, or certain regulatory contexts, this lack of associativity means that simply rerunning the same mathematical operation, even with identical inputs, can yield subtly different numerical outputs unless the exact reduction order is fixed and enforced, which often requires sacrificing some performance benefits that come from flexible parallel execution.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern computers does not obey the mathematical property of associativity, meaning that (a + b) + c may not equal a + (b + c). This fundamental limitation stems from how computers represent real numbers in a finite binary format with limited precision.

The IEEE 754 standard, which governs floating-point computation on virtually all modern hardware, uses a fixed number of bits to store a number's sign, exponent, and mantissa or significand. This finite representation means that not all real numbers can be exactly represented, and operations must round their results to fit within this constraint. When addition occurs, the processor aligns the binary points of the two operands, performs the addition, and then rounds the result back into the representable range. The rounding step is where associativity breaks down.

Consider adding three numbers with vastly different magnitudes. If we compute (a + b) + c where a and b are very small compared to c, the sum a + b might become insignificant when added to c. The accumulated value rounds such that the small contributions vanish entirely. However, if we compute a + (b + c) in a different order, b and c might combine in a way that preserves information differently, or the subsequent addition with a might round differently. Each pathway through the computation produces a slightly different result, all technically correct within the precision guarantees of floating-point, but not identical.

This non-associativity becomes critically important for large matrix multiplications. Computing a matrix product C = A × B requires summing many products together for each element of C. When different computational strategies are employed—whether due to parallelization, different CPU architectures, or varying software implementations—the order in which these products are accumulated changes. A sequential left-to-right reduction follows one reduction order, while a tree-based reduction used in parallel computing follows another order entirely. Both are mathematically correct applications of the floating-point standard, yet they produce different numerical results.

The consequences for reproducibility are severe. If one scientist computes a matrix multiplication using a sequential CPU while another uses a GPU with a different reduction tree structure, or if the same computation runs on different processors with varying capabilities, the results will differ slightly. These differences accumulate through subsequent computations in machine learning pipelines and scientific simulations, eventually producing noticeably different outcomes. For applications requiring bit-for-bit reproducibility—such as validating scientific results or ensuring consistent behavior in safety-critical systems—this characteristic of floating-point arithmetic presents a genuine challenge. Achieving reproducibility requires explicitly controlling the reduction order, which typically means sacrificing the performance benefits of certain parallelization strategies.

# Floating-Point Arithmetic and Non-Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware follows the IEEE 754 standard, which uses a fixed number of bits to represent real numbers. This fundamental constraint creates a mathematical reality that differs from ideal arithmetic: floating-point addition is not associative. The reason lies in how rounding errors accumulate when operations are performed in different orders.

When two floating-point numbers are added, the result is rounded to fit within the available precision. If three numbers are added as (a + b) + c, the intermediate result of a + b is rounded before being added to c. If instead they are added as a + (b + c), then b + c is rounded first, and these two intermediate results differ. The rounding errors introduced in each order are generally different, sometimes significantly so. Because the rounding operation is not distributive over addition in this way, the final results diverge.

This non-associativity becomes increasingly problematic in large matrix multiplications. A matrix multiplication requires computing dot products, where each element of the output matrix is the sum of many products. When the same matrix multiplication is performed with a different reduction order—such as summing products from left to right versus right to left, or using different parallelization strategies—the intermediate results accumulate rounding errors in different patterns. Each different reduction order effectively performs a distinct sequence of rounding operations.

Reproducibility of results across different computational strategies therefore becomes elusive. A matrix multiplication run on a single processor, computing the dot product serially from index zero to n, will produce slightly different results than the same multiplication parallelized across multiple cores, where partial sums from different threads are combined in a different order. Similarly, running the same code twice on the same hardware might yield different results if the compiler optimizes operations differently or if task scheduling changes the order of operations.

For applications requiring bit-for-bit reproducibility—such as numerical weather prediction, scientific simulations where results must be validated against previous runs, or financial computations with strict regulatory requirements—this is deeply problematic. A seemingly trivial change to parallelization strategy or a minor compiler upgrade can alter computed results in ways that are mathematically sound but practically frustrating.

Modern approaches to addressing this challenge include using higher-precision intermediate accumulators, implementing deterministic summation algorithms that enforce a specific reduction order regardless of parallelization, or accepting controlled levels of non-reproducibility as an inherent cost of high-performance computing. Understanding this limitation is essential for anyone developing large-scale numerical code, as it explains why reproducibility cannot be guaranteed without explicit architectural decisions.

Floating-point numbers form a finite subset of the reals: each value is a sign, a bounded exponent, and a fixed-width significand. When two such numbers are added, the exact mathematical sum generally requires more significand bits than the format provides, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. This rounding is where associativity dies. Consider the classic case of adding a very large number, a very small number, and the negation of the large number. If we compute the large number plus the small one first, the small contribution may fall entirely below the least significant bit of the large value and be discarded during rounding; subtracting the large number then yields exactly zero. If instead we add the large number and its negation first, we obtain an exact zero, and adding the small number preserves it perfectly. Two mathematically identical expressions produce different answers, differing by the entire magnitude of the small term. More generally, every addition injects a rounding error whose size is proportional to the magnitude of the intermediate partial sum, so the sequence in which partial sums grow determines the error pattern. Reordering the summands changes the intermediate magnitudes and therefore changes both the individual rounding errors and their accumulation, including whether they partially cancel or reinforce one another. Catastrophic cancellation between nearly equal quantities amplifies the relative significance of earlier rounding decisions, so differences that begin at the level of one unit in the last place can grow to dominate the result when the true sum is close to zero.

Matrix multiplication is nothing but a large collection of dot products, and each dot product is a reduction, a sum of many products. Once a machine has more than one arithmetic unit, implementations gain freedom to split those reductions into chunks and combine partial results in whatever order best exploits registers, cache lines, vector lanes, threads, or accelerator warps. A blocked kernel accumulates over tiles; a vectorized kernel maintains several independent accumulators, one per lane, and folds them together at the end; a multithreaded or GPU kernel splits the contraction dimension across workers whose completion order may itself be nondeterministic. Each of these strategies corresponds to a different parenthesization of the same mathematical sum, and each therefore yields a slightly different floating-point value. Because the choice of strategy depends on matrix dimensions, alignment, thread counts, hardware capabilities, library versions, and whether fused multiply-add instructions are used, the same program can produce bitwise different products on different machines, or even across runs on the same machine when atomic accumulation or dynamic scheduling is involved. The discrepancies are typically tiny in relative terms, but in iterative algorithms they can be amplified over many steps, which is why exact reproducibility usually requires deliberately fixing the reduction order or employing compensated or exactly rounded summation techniques at some cost in performance.

Mathematically, real number addition satisfies (a + b) + c = a + (b + c), but with floating-point numbers this equality can fail, sometimes by a small amount and sometimes, in pathological cases involving cancellation or widely varying magnitudes, by a surprisingly large one.

This lack of associativity becomes especially relevant in large matrix multiplications, since each output element of the product matrix is computed as a sum of many pairwise products, and this sum constitutes a long reduction. On modern hardware, the order in which these products are summed is rarely fixed or predictable. GPUs and multi-core CPUs parallelize the reduction across many threads, tiles, or vector lanes, and the partial sums are combined in whatever order the scheduler, memory layout, or hardware topology dictates. Libraries such as cuBLAS, MKL, or vendor-tuned BLAS implementations may choose different blocking strategies, tile sizes, or accumulation orders depending on matrix dimensions, available hardware resources, or even nondeterministic thread scheduling. This has real consequences for reproducibility. # Floating-Point Addition and Non-Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware operates under the IEEE 754 standard, which represents numbers with finite precision using a fixed number of bits for the mantissa, exponent, and sign. This fundamental constraint creates a mathematical property violation that has profound implications for computational reproducibility: floating-point addition is not associative.

When three numbers are added together, the mathematical property of associativity states that (a + b) + c should equal a + (b + c). In exact arithmetic, this is always true. However, with floating-point numbers, the order of operations matters because each addition operation rounds its result to fit within the available precision. When you add a very large number to a very small number, the small number's contribution may be entirely lost in the rounding process, even though it would have been preserved if added to a different number first.

Consider adding numbers of vastly different magnitudes. If you first add two small numbers together, their sum might become significant enough to influence the final result when added to a larger number. Conversely, if you add the large number to one of the small numbers first, the small number's information gets discarded during rounding, and the second small number then adds to this already-rounded result. The final outcomes differ.

This non-associativity becomes critical in matrix multiplication, particularly in high-performance computing where different reduction orders can be employed. During matrix multiplication, each output element is computed as a dot product, which requires summing many products. When different parallel processors handle different subsets of these products, or when algorithms are restructured for cache efficiency or vectorization, the reduction order changes. A processor might accumulate products in one sequence, while another accumulates them in a different sequence, producing slightly different final results.

In scientific computing, reproducibility refers to obtaining identical results when repeating the same computation. This becomes nearly impossible to guarantee across different hardware configurations, compiler optimizations, or parallel execution strategies, because each variation potentially introduces a different reduction order. The differences might seem negligible at first glance—perhaps differing in the last few decimal places—but they accumulate. In iterative algorithms that depend on previous results, these small differences compound across iterations.

For large-scale matrix multiplications involving millions of operations, even microscopic variations from different reduction orders propagate into noticeably different results. This creates a fundamental tension in computational science: we cannot generally achieve bit-identical reproducibility across different execution strategies without imposing strict sequential ordering, which often requires sacrificing performance. Researchers and engineers must therefore choose between optimized computation and reproducible computation, accepting that truly reproducible results typically require careful algorithmic design that constrains parallelization or restricts precision choices.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so each arithmetic result must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition of two IEEE 754 doubles is computed as if the exact sum were formed and then rounded once, which means the operation is correct to within half an ulp but is not exact. Because rounding depends on the magnitudes of the operands, the error introduced when combining three or more numbers depends on the order in which the partial sums are formed. A classic example: take a large value such as 1e16, then add 1, then subtract 1e16. Adding 1 to 1e16 produces a value whose exact sum cannot be represented, since the spacing between adjacent doubles near 1e16 is 2, so the result rounds back to 1e16 and the subsequent subtraction yields zero. Reassociating the same three terms so that 1e16 and -1e16 cancel first leaves exactly 1. Both answers come from legitimate, individually correctly rounded additions, yet they differ by the entirety of the smaller operand. The general phenomenon is that information carried in the low-order bits of a small addend is destroyed when it is absorbed into a much larger accumulator, and whether that absorption happens depends on grouping. Subtractive cancellation compounds the effect, because catastrophic cancellation can promote a previously negligible rounding error into the leading digits of the result. Consequently addition is commutative in IEEE arithmetic but not associative, and neither is it distributive with multiplication in the exact sense.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, and each dot product is a sum of many products that must be reduced in some order. High performance implementations do not use the naive left-to-right ordering implied by the textbook definition. They tile the computation to fit cache hierarchies, split the contraction dimension across threads or across the lanes of vector registers, use multiple independent accumulators to hide floating-point pipeline latency, and on GPUs assign fragments of the reduction to different warps that combine their partial results through shared memory or atomic operations. Each of these choices imposes a different reduction tree, and by the argument above each tree can yield a numerically different answer. The same library on the same input may therefore return bitwise different results when the number of threads changes, when a different tile size or kernel is selected for a different problem shape, when the hardware supports a wider vector unit, or when nondeterministic scheduling causes atomic contributions to arrive in a varying order. Differences are typically tiny, on the order of the accumulated rounding error, but they can be amplified by ill-conditioned downstream computation, by iterative solvers whose branch decisions depend on comparisons, or by long training runs in which trajectories diverge. Achieving reproducibility therefore requires pinning a fixed reduction order, which usually costs performance, or using compensated or extended-precision accumulation so that the result is order independent to the precision reported.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity in Matrix Multiplication

Floating-point arithmetic on modern computers cannot guarantee the associative property of addition, meaning that (a + b) + c may not equal a + (b + c). This fundamental limitation arises from the finite precision of floating-point representation and the rounding that occurs after each operation.

When two numbers are added, their result must fit into this same fixed format. If the true mathematical result requires more precision than available, the result is rounded according to the IEEE 754 standard, typically using round-to-nearest-even. This rounding error is unavoidable and depends on the magnitude of the operands and their relative differences.

When adding a + b first, the intermediate result is rounded, and then this rounded value is added to c, introducing potentially different rounding than if b and c were added first. Even though both orderings perform the same logical operation, the intermediate rounding steps follow different paths through the space of representable numbers, yielding different final results.

Consider a simple example: adding a very large number, a moderate number, and a very small number. If the small number is added to the large number first, the small number may be entirely lost due to insufficient precision in the significand. However, if the small number is added to the moderate number first, it might contribute to the result before the combination with the large number occurs.

For large matrix multiplications, this issue becomes critical. Matrix multiplication involves computing inner products, where each element of the result requires summing many products of matrix entries. If these partial products are reduced in different orders, the final result differs. This is precisely what happens when the same computation runs on different hardware architectures, uses different numbers of processors, or employs different parallelization strategies.

Modern parallel computing systems typically distribute matrix multiplication work across multiple cores or accelerators. The reduction tree—the order in which partial sums are combined—depends on the specific hardware configuration and scheduling decisions. One machine might combine partial sums left-to-right, while another follows a tree-reduction pattern, and yet another uses a completely different decomposition. Each approach produces slightly different intermediate values and thus different final results.

This non-associativity fundamentally undermines reproducibility. Scientists and engineers cannot rely on getting identical results from the same computation on different systems, or even from the same system with different thread scheduling. This presents real challenges for scientific computing, debugging, and verification, where reproducible results are often essential for validation and understanding.

This finite precision is the root cause of why floating-point addition fails to be associative, a property that mathematicians take for granted in real arithmetic but that breaks down in the digital realm.

When adding three floating-point numbers, the order in which operations are performed typically yields different results. For example, computing (a + b) + c generally produces a different answer than a + (b + c). This happens because each addition operation rounds its result to the nearest representable floating-point value. When numbers of vastly different magnitudes are involved, smaller numbers can be completely lost during rounding. If we add two very large numbers first, their sum might be so large that adding a smaller number afterward causes that smaller number to disappear entirely due to precision limitations. Conversely, if we add the smaller numbers first, we might accumulate more precision before combining with the large number, yielding a different final result.

This non-associativity becomes particularly problematic in large matrix multiplication operations. Matrix multiplication inherently involves computing dot products—long sequences of multiplications followed by additions. A single element in the result matrix requires summing many individual products together. The order in which these products are accumulated directly affects the final value due to the rounding errors introduced at each step.

When different reduction orders are employed, such as summing row-wise versus column-wise, or using different parallelization strategies, the intermediate sums are computed in different sequences. One approach might add smaller products together first before including larger products, while another might interleave large and small products differently. Each ordering introduces slightly different cumulative rounding errors, leading to divergent final answers.

This problem becomes more severe as matrix dimensions increase and more values must be accumulated. With thousands or millions of terms being summed, the accumulated effect of different rounding orders can produce results that differ not just in the last bit, but in several decimal places for single-precision calculations or fewer significant figures for accumulated double-precision errors.

For scientific computing and machine learning applications that rely on reproducibility, this is a significant challenge. Two implementations of the same algorithm using different reduction orders will produce slightly different results, making it impossible to guarantee bit-for-bit identical outcomes. This affects debugging, validation, and the ability to compare results across different hardware platforms or software libraries. Researchers often accept this variability as inherent to floating-point computation, but it remains a fundamental limitation of using finite-precision arithmetic.

# Floating-Point Addition and Non-Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware deviates from the mathematical properties we expect from real numbers. Most critically, addition is not associative: computing (a + b) + c can produce a different result than a + (b + c) when these values are represented as floating-point numbers. This seemingly minor deviation creates profound practical consequences in scientific computing, particularly when performing large-scale matrix multiplications.

The root cause lies in how floating-point numbers are represented and manipulated. Numbers are stored with limited precision, typically 53 bits of significand for double precision. When adding two numbers of vastly different magnitudes, the smaller number may be completely lost due to rounding. Consider adding a very small number to a large one: the small number's contribution might fall entirely below the precision threshold, disappearing from the result. This rounding error depends entirely on the order in which operations occur.

When we compute a matrix multiplication, we are fundamentally performing many dot products, each of which requires summing numerous products. The order in which we accumulate these products directly affects the final answer. Different reduction orders—different sequences of which intermediate sums we combine first—will encounter different rounding errors. Some orders may accumulate errors that partially cancel, while others may compound them. The differences are generally small, but they are real and deterministic yet different.

This issue becomes acute in distributed or parallel computing environments. Consider multiplying two large matrices across multiple processors. One processor might sum its local products from left to right, another from right to left, and a third might employ a binary tree reduction for improved numerical stability. When these partial results are combined, their accumulated rounding errors differ. The final matrix product will therefore differ depending on how the computation was distributed and scheduled.

For reproducibility in scientific applications, this poses a genuine challenge. Running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, with different compiler optimizations, or with different thread scheduling will produce slightly different results due to different reduction orders. These differences seem trivial—often appearing only in the last few decimal places—but they matter enormously for scientific integrity and when results must be exactly reproducible for regulatory compliance or verification purposes.

Some high-performance libraries address this through specialized reduction algorithms designed to control rounding or by using higher-precision accumulators. Others accept that reproducibility requires serialization, sacrificing parallelism to ensure consistent ordering. Understanding this limitation is essential for anyone working with numerical computations on parallel systems, as it reveals a fundamental tension between the benefits of parallelization and the mathematical properties we often take for granted in sequential code.

Floating-point numbers form a finite subset of the reals: each value carries a fixed number of significand bits and an exponent, so most exact sums of two representable numbers are not themselves representable. Hardware therefore rounds every arithmetic result to the nearest representable value. The IEEE-754 standard guarantees that each individual operation is correctly rounded, but nothing guarantees that a chain of correctly rounded operations equals the correctly rounded exact answer. Associativity fails precisely because rounding happens at intermediate steps, and where those steps fall depends on the grouping. The classic illustration uses a large magnitude paired with tiny ones: if x is 10^16 in double precision, then adding 1 to it yields x again, since 1 lies below the spacing between adjacent representable values near 10^16. Computing (x + 1) - x gives zero, while x + (1 - x) gives 1. Cancellation is the other half of the story: subtracting nearly equal quantities destroys leading significant digits, so the relative error inherited from earlier roundings can be amplified enormously, and whether that amplification happens depends entirely on the order in which partial sums accumulate.

Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, and a dot product is a reduction over many products. The mathematical result is a single sum, but the machine must sequence that sum somehow, and modern hardware offers many sequences. A vectorised inner loop keeps several independent accumulators, one per lane of a SIMD register, and combines them only at the end, which is a tree-like grouping rather than a left-to-right one. Multithreaded implementations split the reduction dimension across cores and merge partial results, introducing further regrouping that depends on how many threads happen to be available. Cache-blocking and tiling strategies chop the reduction into panels whose sizes depend on the machine's memory hierarchy and on the matrix dimensions. GPUs add warp-level shuffles and atomic accumulation whose ordering may be nondeterministic from run to run. Fused multiply-add instructions change matters again by omitting the rounding after the multiplication, so a kernel that uses FMA produces different values from one that does not, even with identical grouping.

The practical consequence is that the same linear algebra call, with the same inputs, can return bitwise different answers on different hardware, with different thread counts, with a different library version, or after a compiler upgrade that enables different vectorisation. Differences are typically at the level of a few units in the last place, which is harmless for well-conditioned problems, but they are not harmless for reproducibility claims, for regression tests that compare bits, or for iterative and chaotic computations such as training deep networks or long simulations, where tiny divergences amplify. Remedies include fixing thread counts and library versions, using deterministic reduction modes offered by some libraries, employing compensated or exactly rounded summation algorithms, or accepting tolerance-based comparisons instead of bitwise equality.

This non-associativity becomes particularly problematic in matrix multiplication, an operation that fundamentally requires many additions. A matrix-matrix product requires summing many intermediate products, and the order in which these additions occur can vary significantly depending on how the computation is parallelized or optimized. When a large matrix multiplication is executed with different reduction orders, the floating-point rounding errors accumulate differently each time. One execution path might accumulate small numbers first before adding to larger values, while another might interleave large and small values differently. Each order produces slightly different rounding artifacts that cascade through the computation, producing final results that differ in their least significant digits, and sometimes in more significant digits as well.

This variability undermines reproducibility, a critical requirement in scientific computing. The same matrix multiplication code executed on different systems, with different parallelization strategies, or even recompiled with different compiler flags, can produce numerically different results. While each result is individually valid in the sense that it represents a reasonable approximation of the true mathematical answer, the lack of bitwise reproducibility complicates verification, validation, and debugging of scientific applications that depend on consistent results across multiple runs and platforms.

The result depends crucially on the order in which these products are accumulated.

This non-determinism poses a serious problem for reproducibility. Scientific and engineering applications requiring bit-for-bit reproducibility must carefully control reduction order, sometimes sacrificing performance to ensure consistent results. This constraint on precision is the root cause of why addition loses the associative property that mathematicians expect from real numbers.

When two floating-point numbers are added, the hardware first aligns their exponents, then adds their mantissas. Adding a very large number to a very small number can cause the small number's contribution to be lost entirely due to limited mantissa width, and the order in which operations are performed determines which bits get rounded away.

This phenomenon is not a flaw in hardware design but rather an inherent consequence of representing real numbers with finite precision. Modern processors handle this consistently and predictably within a single execution, but the non-associativity means that mathematically equivalent expressions produce different numerical results.

For large matrix multiplications, this non-associativity becomes highly problematic when reproducibility is required. A matrix multiplication involves computing sums of many products. Depending on how the computation is parallelized or which reduction order is chosen, different intermediate sums are accumulated. One ordering might group partial results differently than another, leading to different rounding operations and ultimately different final answers.

When matrix multiplications are distributed across multiple processors or executed in different computational orders, such as row-wise versus column-wise summation, the accumulated rounding errors diverge. Even a single matrix multiplication executed on different hardware configurations or compiled with different optimization strategies may produce different results, sometimes varying in the last few bits and sometimes showing larger differences depending on the magnitudes of the intermediate values involved.

This creates a genuine challenge for scientific computing applications that require bit-for-bit identical results across different computational platforms or execution strategies. Some approaches to addressing this include using higher-precision intermediate accumulators, enforcing specific reduction orders through careful programming, or accepting that reproducibility across different hardware and compilation strategies may not be achievable. Understanding this limitation is crucial for developing robust numerical software and interpreting the inevitable variations that arise in distributed and parallel computing environments.

Matrix multiplication is nothing but a very large collection of dot products, and each dot product is a reduction over the shared dimension. This discrete representation creates fundamental limitations that make floating-point addition non-associative, meaning that (a + b) + c does not necessarily equal a + (b + c).

The root cause lies in rounding errors introduced during each operation. When two floating-point numbers are added, the hardware performs the addition using higher internal precision, then rounds the result back to the standard floating-point format. The rounding mode, typically round-to-nearest, introduces small errors. Critically, when you add three numbers in different orders, you accumulate rounding errors at different points in the computation, often leading to different final results.

Consider adding a very large number, a medium number, and a very small number. If you add the large and medium numbers first, the small number might lose precision or even become negligible when added to the much larger intermediate result. However, if you first add the medium and small numbers, their combination might retain more precision before being added to the large number. The magnitude differences between operands therefore influence the accumulated rounding error.

For matrix multiplication, this non-associativity becomes especially problematic when using parallel computing. A matrix multiplication requires many accumulated products, typically written as the sum of element-wise products from corresponding rows and columns. The order in which these products are accumulated dramatically affects the final result due to cascading rounding errors. A straightforward left-to-right reduction follows one error accumulation pattern, while a tree-based reduction used in parallel computing follows a completely different pattern by grouping partial sums hierarchically.

When different computational resources or different orderings are used, the reduction order changes. One processor might accumulate results left-to-right, another might use a tree structure, and a third might batch results differently. Each approach generates its own sequence of rounding errors, leading to slightly different final answers. These differences typically appear in the last few bits of the floating-point representation, but they are absolutely reproducible given the same reduction order and deterministic hardware behavior.

This creates a significant challenge for scientific computing and machine learning applications. Developers cannot assume that running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware configurations, or even running the same code with different thread counts, will produce identical results. For reproducibility in research and production systems, either the reduction order must be rigorously controlled, or results must be compared using approximate equality rather than exact matching. This tension between performance optimization through parallelization and bit-exact reproducibility remains a fundamental issue in numerical computing.

# Floating-Point Addition and Non-Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware deviates fundamentally from the mathematical properties we expect from real numbers. One of the most consequential deviations is that addition is not associative: computing (a + b) + c does not necessarily yield the same result as a + (b + c). This seemingly abstract mathematical property has profound practical implications for scientific computing, particularly when performing operations on large matrices.

The root cause lies in the finite precision of floating-point representation. Modern computers typically use IEEE 754 double-precision numbers, which store only about 15–17 significant decimal digits. When adding two numbers of vastly different magnitudes, the smaller number's least significant digits fall below the precision threshold and are effectively lost. The order in which numbers are added therefore determines which values get rounded away. For instance, adding a huge number to a tiny number and then to another tiny number produces a different result than adding the two tiny numbers first, because in the latter case their sum might be large enough to retain more precision before adding the huge number.

This becomes catastrophic at scale in matrix multiplication. Computing a matrix product C = AB requires summing many partial products for each element of C. A naive approach might accumulate these products in a fixed order, but modern parallel and distributed systems rarely respect a single canonical order. Different execution paths—whether due to thread scheduling, processor availability, or deliberate algorithmic choices—naturally lead to different reduction orders where intermediate results are combined in different sequences.

Consider a matrix multiplication distributed across multiple processors. One processor might compute partial sums in one order while another uses a different order due to load balancing or communication patterns. Even on a single machine, compiler optimizations and SIMD vectorization can reorder operations in ways the programmer didn't explicitly specify. Each valid execution path produces slightly different floating-point results due to accumulated rounding errors varying with the reduction order.

The consequences for reproducibility are severe. Running the same matrix multiplication code twice can produce different answers, even on identical hardware. This makes debugging difficult, complicates numerical validation, and frustrates scientists who expect deterministic results. For applications requiring exact reproducibility—such as validating scientific results, maintaining audit trails, or debugging numerical instabilities—this is profoundly problematic.

Addressing this requires conscious effort. Some approaches include enforcing a specific reduction order at the cost of parallelism, using higher precision arithmetic for accumulation, or employing specialized algorithms that minimize error growth regardless of order. The fundamental tension remains: faster, more parallel computation typically sacrifices reproducibility, while guaranteeing reproducibility often demands sequential or restricted computation patterns that underutilize modern hardware capabilities.

Achieving reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, or using compensated summation, higher-precision accumulation, or pre-rounding techniques that make the result order-independent, all of which cost performance.

Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers using a finite number of bits, typically following the IEEE 754 standard, which allocates a fixed-size mantissa to store significant digits. When two floating-point numbers of very different magnitudes are added, the smaller number must be shifted to align its exponent with the larger one, and in doing so, some of its low-order bits fall off the end of the mantissa and are rounded or truncated. This rounding introduces a small error at each addition step. Because the amount of error depends on the specific pair of numbers being combined at each stage, the order in which numbers are summed changes which values get rounded and by how much. Mathematically, real-number addition is associative—(a+b)+c always equals a+(b+c)—but in floating-point arithmetic these two expressions can yield different results because the intermediate rounding differs depending on grouping.

This becomes especially relevant in large matrix multiplications, where each output element is computed as a sum of many products, often thousands or millions of terms in deep learning or scientific computing contexts. The mathematical result of this sum does not depend on the order of addition, but the floating-point result does. Modern hardware—CPUs, GPUs, and specialized accelerators—exploits parallelism to speed up these reductions, using techniques like tree reduction, blocked summation, vectorized SIMD operations, or accumulation across multiple threads or cores. Each of these strategies groups partial sums differently. A GPU might split a dot product across many threads, each accumulating a subset of terms in parallel before combining partial sums, while a CPU might process values sequentially or in different-sized batches depending on cache and vectorization width. Since the reduction order varies with the number of threads, tile sizes, batching strategy, or even the specific hardware generation being used, the accumulated rounding errors differ correspondingly.

The consequence is that the same matrix multiplication, performed with mathematically identical inputs, can produce slightly different numerical outputs depending on the hardware, the library implementation, the number of parallel threads, or even runtime scheduling variations that alter reduction order between one execution and the next. While these differences are usually tiny—on the order of machine epsilon per operation—they can accumulate over many operations, especially in iterative algorithms like neural network training, where small early discrepancies can compound over many layers and training steps. This makes bitwise reproducibility across different hardware, or even across repeated runs on the same hardware with nondeterministic parallel reduction, difficult to guarantee, which matters for debugging, scientific verification, and certain regulatory or safety-critical contexts requiring exact reproducibility.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so each arithmetic result must be rounded to the nearest representable value. IEEE 754 addition is correctly rounded, meaning it computes the exact sum and then snaps it to the nearest double (or float), but that rounding step is where associativity dies. When you compute (a + b) + c, the intermediate a + b is rounded before c is added, discarding information that would have mattered had c been included first. Compute a + (b + c) and a different piece of information is discarded. The classic illustration uses widely separated magnitudes: with double precision, (1e16 + 1.0) rounds back to 1e16 because 1.0 falls below the spacing between adjacent representable values near 1e16, so adding -1e16 afterward yields zero, whereas 1e16 + (1.0 - 1e16) yields exactly 1.0. Each individual operation is as accurate as the format allows; the discrepancy is purely an artifact of when rounding happens relative to cancellation and magnitude disparity. The same effect makes addition non-associative even in benign cases, where results differ only in the last bit or two, but those tiny differences are still bit-level differences.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a huge collection of dot products, and every dot product is a reduction — a summation over the contraction index. Modern hardware and libraries never perform that summation in the naive left-to-right order. They tile the computation to fit caches, split the contraction index across SIMD lanes that accumulate partial sums independently, unroll loops into several accumulator registers to hide latency, fuse multiply and add so that products are rounded only once, use tensor or matrix cores with their own internal accumulation trees and sometimes wider internal precision, and on GPUs may split the reduction across many threads or blocks whose partial results are combined atomically in whatever order they finish. Every one of these choices imposes a different parenthesization of the same mathematical sum, and by non-associativity each can produce a numerically different answer.

The practical consequence is that the "same" matrix multiplication can yield bit-different results when the number of threads changes, when the library selects a different kernel because the matrix shape or alignment changed, when it runs on a different CPU with wider vectors or a different GPU generation, or simply when nondeterministic atomic ordering shuffles the accumulation. The differences start near the rounding-error level, roughly the machine epsilon times the magnitude of the terms times the square root or the count of accumulated terms, but iterative or chaotic computations amplify them: training a neural network, running a solver, or branching on a comparison can turn a last-bit disagreement into visibly divergent outcomes. Bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, or using compensated, extended-precision, or exactly-rounded summation schemes that make the result order-independent — usually at some cost in speed.
